body.en: Unit 1 examines polynomial and rational functions through the lens of rates of change and function behavior — the conceptual language of calculus. Emphasis is placed on concavity, zeros, asymptotes, and algebraic transformations.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Polynomial Degree, Factoring, Zeros & End Behavior

body.en: Analyze polynomial structure, identify zeros and their multiplicities, and determine global end behavior using the leading term test.

figure.title: Unit 1 · Polynomial and Rational Functions — Function Curve & Symmetry Analysis

caption.en: Parabola \(f(x) = (x - 3)^{2} - 4\) with vertex at \((3, -4)\) and symmetry reference line \(y = x\).

body.en:
End behavior is governed strictly by the leading term \(a_nx^n\):

Leading termLeft end (\(x \to -\infty\))Right end (\(x \to +\infty\))
\(a_n>0,\;n\) even\(\to+\infty\)\(\to+\infty\)
\(a_n<0,\;n\) even\(\to-\infty\)\(\to-\infty\)
\(a_n>0,\;n\) odd\(\to-\infty\)\(\to+\infty\)
\(a_n<0,\;n\) odd\(\to+\infty\)\(\to-\infty\)

Multiplicity of zeros: If \((x-c)^m\) is a factor of \(p(x)\):

  • When \(m\) is odd, the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis. If \(m > 1\) (e.g., \(m = 3\)), the curve flattens as it traverses the intercept.
  • When \(m\) is even (e.g., \(m = 2\)), the graph touches the \(x\)-axis and turns around (bounces) without crossing.

Division Algorithm: For any polynomial \(p(x)\) and non-zero divisor \(d(x)\), there exist unique polynomials \(q(x)\) (quotient) and \(r(x)\) (remainder) such that \[ p(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x), \quad \text{where } \deg(r) < \deg(d) \text{ or } r(x) \equiv 0. \]

Remainder Theorem & Proof: If \(d(x) = x - c\), then \(\deg(r) < 1\), so \(r(x) = R\) (a constant). Evaluating at \(x = c\): \[ p(c) = (c - c)q(c) + R = 0 \cdot q(c) + R = R. \] Hence, dividing \(p(x)\) by \((x - c)\) yields a remainder equal to \(p(c)\).

Factor Theorem: A linear binomial \((x - c)\) is a factor of \(p(x)\) if and only if \(p(c) = 0\).

Rational Zero Theorem: If \(p(x) = a_nx^n + \dots + a_0\) has integer coefficients, any rational zero has the form \(\pm \frac{p}{q}\), where \(p\) is a factor of constant term \(a_0\) and \(q\) is a factor of leading coefficient \(a_n\).

label.en: ● Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) & AP 3-Step Justification Protocol

body.en:
Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT): If \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) and \(d\) is any real number strictly between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), then there exists at least one number \(c \in (a, b)\) such that \(f(c) = d\).

College Board 3-Step Scoring Checklist:

  1. State Continuity: Explicitly declare that the function is continuous on the closed interval \([a, b]\) (e.g. 'Since \(p(x)\) is a polynomial, it is continuous on \([a, b]\)').
  2. Show the Inequality: Demonstrate that the target value lies between the boundary outputs (e.g. '\(p(1) = -4 < 0 < 5 = p(2)\)').
  3. Conclude with IVT: Invoke the theorem directly: 'Therefore, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there exists at least one \(c \in (1, 2)\) such that \(p(c) = 0\)'.

Find all real zeros and state their multiplicities for \(p(x)=x^4-2x^3-3x^2\). Describe the end behavior using limit notation.

Factor by pulling out the GCF: \[ p(x)=x^2(x^2-2x-3)=x^2(x-3)(x+1). \]

Zeros: \(x=0\) (multiplicity 2 — graph bounces), \(x=3\) (multiplicity 1 — graph crosses), and \(x=-1\) (multiplicity 1 — graph crosses).

End behavior: The degree \(n=4\) is even and the leading coefficient \(a_4=1>0\), so \[ \lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=+\infty \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=+\infty. \]

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Unit 1 · Polynomial and Rational Functions (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): When the integer \( P = 31 \) is divided by \( Q = 7 \), the division algorithm gives \( P = Qq + r \) with \( 0 \le r < Q \). What is the remainder \( r \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: Since \( 31 = 7 \times 4 + 3 \), the remainder is \( r = 3 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Unit 1 · Polynomial and Rational Functions)

rows.en: Confuses the product law \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\) with a non-existent sum rule.
Only factor products, quotients, and powers inside logarithms: \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\).
Keeping both roots of \(\sqrt{2x+3} = x - 3\) without checking \(x - 3 \ge 0\)
Squaring both sides loses the sign of \(x - {r}\), introducing roots where \(\sqrt{\cdot} = -\text{number}\).
Enforce the range condition \(x \ge 3\) before or after squaring.
Restricting domain of \(f(x) = (x-3)^2 + 1\) to \(x \ge 0\) for invertibility
The vertex is at \(x = 3\), so \(f(2) = f(4) = 2\) fails the horizontal line test on \(x \ge 0\).
Restrict the domain at the vertex axis of symmetry: \(x \ge 3\) (or \(x \le 3\)).

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Let \(q(x) = -(x+2)^2(x-1)(x-4)^3\). What is the degree of \(q(x)\), does the graph cross or touch the \(x\)-axis at \(x = -2\), and what is \(\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x)\)?

solution.en:
Sum the exponents of the linear factors to find the degree: \[ 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 \implies \text{degree } 6. \]

At \(x = -2\), the multiplicity is 2 (even), so the graph touches the \(x\)-axis and turns around without crossing.

The degree is even (6) and the leading coefficient is negative (\(-1\)), so \[ \lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = -\infty. \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 \implies \text{degree } 6. \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Average Rate of Change, Concavity & Inflection Points

body.en: Compute average rates of change over specified intervals and determine concavity transitions from the behavior of consecutive rates of change.

The average rate of change (AROC) of \(f\) over \([a,b]\) is the secant line slope: \[ \text{AROC}_{[a, b]} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. \]

Concavity via Rate of Change:

  • If the AROC is increasing over consecutive equal-length intervals as \(x\) moves to the right, the function is concave up.
  • If the AROC is decreasing over consecutive equal-length intervals, the function is concave down.
  • An inflection point is a point on the graph where the function is continuous and concavity changes from upward to downward (or vice versa).

label.en: ● Proof: Quadratic Functions Have Strictly Constant Second Differences

body.en:
Let \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) with \(a \neq 0\), and let \(h > 0\) be a constant step size.

Step 1: Compute first differences \(\Delta f(x)\): \[ \Delta f(x) = f(x+h) - f(x) = a(x+h)^2 + b(x+h) + c - (ax^2 + bx + c) \] \[ = a(x^2 + 2hx + h^2) + bx + bh + c - ax^2 - bx - c = 2ahx + ah^2 + bh. \]

Step 2: Compute second differences \(\Delta^2 f(x)\): \[ \Delta^2 f(x) = \Delta f(x+h) - \Delta f(x) = [2ah(x+h) + ah^2 + bh] - [2ahx + ah^2 + bh] = 2ah^2. \]

Conclusion: The quantity \(2ah^2\) is independent of \(x\). Thus, any quadratic function produces strictly constant second differences for equally spaced inputs. Consequently, the rate of change changes at a constant rate, meaning concavity is invariant: concave up everywhere if \(a > 0\) and concave down everywhere if \(a < 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

body.en:
Calculate the average rate of change of \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\) over \([0, 1]\) and \([1, 2]\). Use these values to estimate whether \(f\) is concave up or concave down on \([0, 2]\).

For \([0, 1]\): \[ \text{AROC} = \frac{f(1) - f(0)}{1 - 0} = \frac{(1 - 3) - 0}{1} = -2. \]

For \([1, 2]\): \[ \text{AROC} = \frac{f(2) - f(1)}{2 - 1} = \frac{(8 - 6) - (-2)}{1} = \frac{2 + 2}{1} = 4. \]

Because the AROC increases from \(-2\) to \(4\) as the interval shifts to the right, \(f(x)\) is concave up on \([0, 2]\).

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

The function \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 2\) has a local maximum and a local minimum. Determine the intervals on which \(f\) is concave up and concave down, and find the coordinates of the inflection point.

solution.en:
The rate of change switches from decreasing to increasing at the inflection point. Taking the second derivative (or analyzing symmetric rates of change): \[ f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9, \quad f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 0 \implies x = 1. \]

For \(x < 1\), \(f''(x) < 0\), so \(f\) is concave down on \((-\infty, 1)\).

For \(x > 1\), \(f''(x) > 0\), so \(f\) is concave up on \((1, \infty)\).

The inflection point is \((1, f(1)) = (1, 1 - 3 - 9 + 2) = \mathbf{(1, -9)}\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Unit 1 · Polynomial and Rational Functions and start from \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 2\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9, \quad f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 0 \implies x = 1. \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Rational Functions: Holes, Asymptotes & Limit Behavior

body.en: Deconstruct rational functions by canceling common factors to find removable discontinuities, and evaluate end-behavior limits and vertical asymptote behaviors.

label.en: ● Rational Function Asymptotes, Holes & Limit Derivations

body.en:
Let \(R(x) = \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \dfrac{a_n x^n + \dots + a_0}{b_d x^d + \dots + b_0}\) be a rational function with numerator degree \(n\) and denominator degree \(d\):

  • Removable Discontinuity (Hole): Occurs at \(x = c\) if \((x - c)\) is a factor of both \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) with multiplicity in \(p(x)\) greater than or equal to that in \(q(x)\). The two-sided limit \(\lim_{x \to c} R(x) = L\) exists and is finite; the hole is at coordinate \((c, L)\).
  • Vertical Asymptote: Occurs at \(x = a\) where \(q(a) = 0\) after all common factors have been canceled. At least one one-sided limit approaches \(\pm\infty\): \[ \lim_{x \to a^-} R(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to a^+} R(x) = \pm\infty. \]
  • Horizontal Asymptote: Governed by end-behavior limits as \(x \to \pm\infty\):
    • If \(n < d\): \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} R(x) = 0 \implies y = 0\).
    • If \(n = d\): \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} R(x) = \frac{a_n}{b_d} \implies y = \frac{a_n}{b_d}\).
    • If \(n > d\): No horizontal asymptote exists.
  • Slant (Oblique) Asymptote: If \(n = d + 1\), polynomial long division yields: \[ R(x) = (mx + b) + \frac{r(x)}{q(x)}, \quad \text{where } \deg(r) < d. \] Because \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{r(x)}{q(x)} = 0\), we have: \[ \lim_{x \to \pm\infty} [R(x) - (mx + b)] = 0. \] Thus the line \(y = mx + b\) is a slant asymptote.

label.en: ● The 3-Part Definition of Continuity at a Point & Complete Taxonomy of Graph Cases

body.en:
A function \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) if and only if all three conditions of the Continuity Checklist are satisfied:

  1. Condition 1: \(f(c)\) is defined (meaning \(c\) is in the domain of \(f\)).
  2. Condition 2: \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)\) exists (meaning left and right limits are finite and agree: \(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L\)).
  3. Condition 3: \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = f(c)\) (the limiting trend matches the actual output).

Failure of any condition produces a specific discontinuity geometry on the Cartesian plane:

  • Case 1 · Continuous: All 3 conditions hold. The curve passes unbroken through \((c, f(c))\).
  • Case 2 · Removable (Hole): Condition 1 fails (undefined at \(c\)), but Condition 2 holds (limit \(L\) exists). The graph has an open ring at \((c, L)\).
  • Case 3 · Removable (Displaced Point): Conditions 1 and 2 hold, but Condition 3 fails (\(f(c) \neq L\)). An open ring sits at \((c, L)\) while a solid dot sits at \((c, f(c))\).
  • Case 4 · Jump Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because one-sided limits are finite but unequal (\(\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x\to c^+} f(x)\)). A step break occurs in the graph.
  • Case 5 · Infinite Discontinuity (Vertical Asymptote): Condition 2 fails because one or both one-sided limits grow without bound to \(\pm\infty\).
  • Case 6 · Essential / Oscillating Discontinuity: Condition 2 fails because function values oscillate infinitely rapidly between bounds as \(x\) approaches \(c\).

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Polynomial & Rational Functions

body.en:
• Hole vs. Vertical Asymptote: If \((x-c)\) cancels out, \(x=c\) is a hole, NOT an asymptote. You must state the \((x, y)\) coordinates of the hole.
  • Multiplicity at Zeros: Odd multiplicity crosses; even multiplicity touches and bounces. An odd multiplicity greater than 1 (e.g. \(m=3\)) flattens as it crosses.
  • Limit Notation for End Behavior: Always state end behavior with proper limits: \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L\), not informal arrow notation.
  • Slant Asymptotes: When \(\deg(p) = \deg(q) + 1\), perform polynomial long division. The quotient polynomial \(y = mx + b\) is the slant asymptote; discard the remainder.

Fully analyze \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-9}{x^2+x-6}\): identify holes, vertical asymptotes, horizontal asymptotes, and \(x\)-intercepts.

Step 1: Factor numerator and denominator: \[ f(x)=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x+3)(x-2)}. \]

Step 2: Cancel common factor \((x+3)\): Hole at \(x=-3\). The simplified expression is \(\dfrac{x-3}{x-2}\) for \(x \neq -3\). Substitute \(x = -3\): \[ y = \frac{-3-3}{-3-2} = \frac{-6}{-5} = \frac{6}{5} \implies \text{Hole at }\left(-3, \frac{6}{5}\right). \]

Step 3: Vertical asymptote from remaining denominator zero: \(x = 2\).

Step 4: Horizontal asymptote: Since degrees are equal (\(n=d=2\)), \(y = \frac{1}{1} = 1\). \(x\)-intercept where numerator equals zero: \(x = 3\).

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Let \(R(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 - 8}{x^2 - 5x + 6}\). (a) Find the domain of \(R(x)\). (b) Identify any holes and state their coordinates. (c) Write the equations of all vertical and horizontal asymptotes.

solution.en:
(a) Domain: Factor the denominator: \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3)\). Thus the domain is all real numbers except \(x eq 2\) and \(x eq 3\), or \((-\infty, 2) \cup (2, 3) \cup (3, \infty)\).

(b) Holes: Factor the numerator: \(2(x^2 - 4) = 2(x - 2)(x + 2)\). The factor \((x - 2)\) cancels: \[ R(x) = rac{2(x + 2)}{x - 3} \quad (x eq 2). \] Evaluating at \(x = 2\): \[ y = rac{2(2 + 2)}{2 - 3} = rac{8}{-1} = -8. \] Hole coordinates: \((2, -8)\).

(c) Asymptotes: Vertical asymptote at the remaining denominator zero: \(x = 3\). Degrees of numerator and denominator are both 2, so the horizontal asymptote is \(y = 2\).
